--- title: "Regression for counts" description: "Poisson regression predicts a count on the log scale, so it never falls below zero; the negative binomial allows for counts that vary more than Poisson expects." order: 3 categories: [supervised, regression] --- ## A count never falls below zero The curve on [Linear and polynomial regression](linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd) found a peak in the survey's count and then predicted fewer than zero animals. This page introduces Poisson regression, which predicts a count on a log scale and so can never go below zero, and shows how to read its coefficients as multipliers. It then checks one assumption Poisson makes that counts of animals rarely meet, and relaxes it with the negative binomial. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Predicting the log of the count Poisson regression keeps the weighted sum of linear regression, a starting value plus a fixed amount for each input, but uses it to predict the logarithm of the expected count, $\hat{\mu}$ (the average count for those inputs): $$\log(\hat{\mu}) = a + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots \qquad\text{so}\qquad \hat{\mu} = e^{a + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots}$$ $e$ raised to any power is above zero, so the prediction can come close to zero but never cross it. Nothing is cut off afterwards; the shape of the model rules negative counts out. Adding an amount to a logarithm multiplies the number itself, so each coefficient becomes a **multiplier** once raised as a power of $e$. A coefficient of 0.4 means each extra unit of the input multiplies the expected count by $e^{0.4}$ = 1.49, whether the count is 2 or 200. A coefficient of 0 gives a multiplier of 1, no change, and a negative one a multiplier below 1. A squared input works as it did for linear regression: the curve has one peak, still at $-b / 2c$. ## Counts that vary more than Poisson expects Poisson regression also assumes how widely the counts scatter around the expected count: their variance equals it. Where the model expects 4 animals, the counts should have a variance of about 4; where it expects 20, about 20. Animals that gather in groups vary more than that, as [Regression and classification](regression-and-classification.qmd) found for the survey. This is **overdispersion**. The predictions are still sensible, but the model treats the data as more certain than they are, so its confidence intervals are too narrow. The **negative binomial** is a count model with one extra number, $\theta$ (theta), for the extra spread: the smaller $\theta$, the more the counts vary beyond what Poisson expects. Its predictions follow the same kind of curve. ::: {.diagram} ![Linear regression models the count itself and can fall below zero. Poisson regression is a straight line in the log of the count, so the count nears zero but never crosses it. The negative binomial keeps the curve and allows a wider spread.](img/counts-model.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Linear regression, the count itself: count equals a plus b times the input; a straight line through falling counts crosses a dashed line marking zero; a straight line in the count keeps falling, even below zero. Poisson regression, a straight line in the log: count equals e to the power a plus b times the input; a curve falls towards the zero line and levels off above it; each unit multiplies the count, so the curve nears zero but never crosses it. Negative binomial, room for extra spread: the same rising curve with two shaded bands, a narrow one for Poisson and a wider one for the negative binomial, both growing as the count grows; counts of animals that gather in groups vary more than Poisson expects. A note says a count never falls below zero, and its spread grows with its size."} ::: ## Worked example The data, the split by site and the recipe with squared depth and temperature are those of [Linear and polynomial regression](linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd). Each seabed type is compared with sand, which `step_relevel()` makes the baseline, and each season with spring. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season line_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_relevel(substrate, ref_level = "sand") curve_recipe <- line_recipe |> step_poly(depth_m, temperature_c, degree = 2, options = list(raw = TRUE)) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, PolynomialFeatures from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train, test = survey.iloc[train_rows], survey.iloc[test_rows] # The dropped level of each column is its baseline: sand, and spring as in R. dummies = OneHotEncoder(drop=["sand", "spring"], sparse_output=False) line_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", dummies, categorical), ]) def squared(column): return (column, Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)), ]), [column]) curve_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ squared("depth_m"), squared("temperature_c"), ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]), ("categorical", dummies, categorical), ]) # scikit-learn's PoissonRegressor gives no confidence intervals, so the count # models come from statsmodels, fitted on the recipe's output. prepared = curve_recipe.fit(train[predictors]) def design(data): columns = pd.DataFrame(prepared.transform(data[predictors]), columns=prepared.get_feature_names_out(), index=data.index) return sm.add_constant(columns) ``` ::: ::: ### The Poisson curve In tidymodels, Poisson regression is `poisson_reg()`, from the poissonreg package; it takes the same recipe as linear regression. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poisson_fit <- workflow(curve_recipe, poisson_reg()) |> fit(train) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} poisson_fit = sm.GLM(train["abundance"], design(train), family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit() ``` ::: ::: The Poisson curve puts the temperature peak at 8.4 °C, close to the 7.5 °C of the linear regression curve. The two part company after the peak. The linear regression curve falls ever faster and crosses zero; the Poisson curve levels off towards zero and stays above it. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} grid <- tibble( temperature_c = seq(temp_range[1], temp_range[2], length.out = 200), depth_m = median(train$depth_m, na.rm = TRUE), chlorophyll_mg_m3 = median(train$chlorophyll_mg_m3, na.rm = TRUE), salinity_psu = median(train$salinity_psu, na.rm = TRUE), substrate = factor("sand", levels = levels(train$substrate)), season = factor("summer", levels = levels(train$season)) ) curves <- bind_rows( augment(line_fit, grid) |> mutate(model = "Straight line"), augment(curve_fit, grid) |> mutate(model = "Curve"), augment(poisson_fit, grid) |> mutate(model = "Poisson curve") ) ggplot(curves, aes(temperature_c, .pred, colour = model)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.6) + geom_rug(data = train, aes(temperature_c), inherit.aes = FALSE, sides = "b", alpha = 0.3, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Straight line" = ml_palette[["blue"]], "Curve" = ml_palette[["orange"]], "Poisson curve" = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]), breaks = c("Straight line", "Curve", "Poisson curve")) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Predicted count", colour = NULL, title = "The Poisson curve levels off above zero") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The predicted count across the survey's temperatures, with the other inputs held at their typical values (sand, summer, median depth, chlorophyll and salinity). The ticks along the bottom are the training stations. The two linear regression models are those of the previous page; the Poisson curve finds a similar peak and levels off above zero in warm water.](count-regression_files/figure-html/fig-shapes-1.png){#fig-shapes fig-alt='Three lines of predicted count against temperature, with a horizontal line marking zero and ticks along the bottom showing the temperatures of the training stations. The straight line declines slowly. The linear regression curve rises to a peak in the middle of the range, then falls steeply and crosses zero before the warm end. The Poisson curve rises to a similar peak, then falls more gently and flattens just above zero.' width=1500} ::: ::: ### Reading the coefficients as multipliers `exponentiate = TRUE` turns each coefficient into its multiplier. Each comes with a **95% confidence interval**: the range of multipliers the data are consistent with. An interval that stays on one side of 1 says the data can tell that level from the baseline; one that includes 1 says they cannot. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} multipliers <- function(fitted) { tidy(fitted, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |> filter(str_detect(term, "substrate|season")) |> transmute(term, multiplier = estimate, conf_low = conf.low, conf_high = conf.high) } multipliers(poisson_fit) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | multiplier| conf_low| conf_high| |:---------------|----------:|--------:|---------:| |substrategravel | 1.15| 1.03| 1.29| |substratemud | 1.34| 1.22| 1.47| |substraterock | 0.78| 0.65| 0.93| |seasonsummer | 1.34| 1.07| 1.66| |seasonautumn | 1.09| 0.96| 1.23| |seasonwinter | 0.87| 0.72| 1.05|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def multipliers(fitted): interval = np.exp(fitted.conf_int()) table = pd.DataFrame({ "term": fitted.params.index, "multiplier": np.exp(fitted.params).round(2).to_numpy(), "conf_low": interval[0].round(2).to_numpy(), "conf_high": interval[1].round(2).to_numpy(), }) return table[table["term"].str.contains("substrate|season")].reset_index(drop=True) multipliers(poisson_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | term | multiplier | conf_low | conf_high | |:------------------------------|-------------:|-----------:|------------:| | categorical__substrate_gravel | 1.14 | 1.01 | 1.3 | | categorical__substrate_mud | 1.37 | 1.24 | 1.52 | | categorical__substrate_rock | 0.73 | 0.59 | 0.89 | | categorical__season_autumn | 1.18 | 1.03 | 1.35 | | categorical__season_summer | 2.19 | 1.73 | 2.76 | | categorical__season_winter | 0.64 | 0.52 | 0.79 | ::: ::: ::: With the other inputs held fixed, a muddy station is expected to hold 1.34 times the count of a sandy one, with an interval from 1.22 to 1.47. A rocky one is expected to hold 0.78 times as many, fewer than on sand, and its interval, 0.65 to 0.93, stays below 1. Taken at face value, the data tell both mud and rock apart from sand. The next check shows how far to trust these intervals. ### Checking the spread For each station, square the gap between the count and the prediction and divide by the prediction, which is what Poisson expects that squared gap to be on average. If Poisson is right, the average of these, taken over the stations less one for each coefficient, is about 1. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poisson_glm <- extract_fit_engine(poisson_fit) sum(residuals(poisson_glm, type = "pearson")^2) / poisson_glm$df.residual ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 3.70927 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} poisson_fit.pearson_chi2 / poisson_fit.df_resid ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> np.float64(3.557071454023707) ``` ::: ::: ::: The ratio is 3.7: after the inputs have explained what they can, the counts still vary about 3.7 times as much as Poisson expects. The predictions can stand, but the intervals above are too narrow. ### The negative binomial parsnip has no negative binomial model, so it comes from the MASS package. The recipe is still used: `prep()` estimates it on the training data and `bake()` applies it, as in [Scaling and encoding](../02-marine-data/scaling-and-encoding.qmd), and `MASS::glm.nb()` is fitted on the result. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prepared <- prep(curve_recipe) nb_fit <- MASS::glm.nb(abundance ~ ., data = bake(prepared, new_data = NULL)) nb_fit$theta ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 1.45583 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # sm.NegativeBinomial estimates the extra spread alongside the coefficients, # as glm.nb() does; it reports alpha, which is 1 / theta. nb_fit = sm.NegativeBinomial(train["abundance"], design(train)).fit( method="newton", disp=0) 1 / nb_fit.params["alpha"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> np.float64(1.4444571326651994) ``` ::: ::: ::: The two models' intervals, side by side: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} left_join(multipliers(poisson_fit), multipliers(nb_fit), by = "term", suffix = c("_poisson", "_negbin")) |> select(term, starts_with("conf")) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | conf_low_poisson| conf_high_poisson| conf_low_negbin| conf_high_negbin| |:---------------|----------------:|-----------------:|---------------:|----------------:| |substrategravel | 1.03| 1.29| 0.96| 1.54| |substratemud | 1.22| 1.47| 1.16| 1.71| |substraterock | 0.65| 0.93| 0.63| 1.29| |seasonsummer | 1.07| 1.66| 0.83| 2.07| |seasonautumn | 0.96| 1.23| 0.81| 1.37| |seasonwinter | 0.72| 1.05| 0.56| 1.19|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} both = multipliers(poisson_fit).merge( multipliers(nb_fit), on="term", suffixes=("_poisson", "_negbin")) both.filter(regex="term|conf") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | term | conf_low_poisson | conf_high_poisson | conf_low_negbin | conf_high_negbin | |:------------------------------|-------------------:|--------------------:|------------------:|-------------------:| | categorical__substrate_gravel | 1.01 | 1.3 | 0.91 | 1.5 | | categorical__substrate_mud | 1.24 | 1.52 | 1.12 | 1.66 | | categorical__substrate_rock | 0.59 | 0.89 | 0.5 | 1.04 | | categorical__season_autumn | 1.03 | 1.35 | 0.86 | 1.53 | | categorical__season_summer | 1.73 | 2.76 | 1.27 | 3.39 | | categorical__season_winter | 0.52 | 0.79 | 0.41 | 0.94 | ::: ::: ::: $\theta$ is 1.46, a lot of extra spread. The multipliers barely move, but every interval widens, on average to 2.1 times its Poisson width. Mud's interval, 1.16 to 1.71, still stays above 1. Rock's, 0.63 to 1.29, now includes 1: allowing for the extra spread, the data can no longer tell rock from sand. The Poisson model was sure of a difference the data do not support. ### The four compared on new sites The same scores as on the previous page, on the same test sites. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} score <- function(predicted, label) { tibble( model = label, rmse = rmse_vec(test$abundance, predicted), rsq = rsq_vec(test$abundance, predicted), lowest = min(predicted), below_zero = sum(predicted < 0) ) } scores <- bind_rows( score(predict(line_fit, test)$.pred, "Straight line"), score(predict(curve_fit, test)$.pred, "Curve"), score(predict(poisson_fit, test)$.pred, "Poisson"), score(predict(nb_fit, bake(prepared, new_data = test), type = "response"), "Negative binomial") ) scores |> mutate(across(rmse:lowest, \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | rmse| rsq| lowest| below_zero| |:-----------------|----:|----:|------:|----------:| |Straight line | 3.75| 0.15| -0.40| 1| |Curve | 3.62| 0.22| -3.86| 12| |Poisson | 3.55| 0.24| 0.23| 0| |Negative binomial | 3.54| 0.25| 0.23| 0|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error def linear(recipe): fitted = Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", LinearRegression())]).fit( train[predictors], train["abundance"]) return fitted.predict(test[predictors]) def score(predicted, label): predicted = np.asarray(predicted) truth = test["abundance"] return { "model": label, "rmse": round(root_mean_squared_error(truth, predicted), 2), "rsq": round(np.corrcoef(predicted, truth)[0, 1] ** 2, 2), "lowest": round(predicted.min(), 2), "below_zero": int((predicted < 0).sum()), } pd.DataFrame([ score(linear(line_recipe), "Straight line"), score(linear(curve_recipe), "Curve"), score(poisson_fit.predict(design(test)), "Poisson"), score(nb_fit.predict(design(test)), "Negative binomial"), ]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | rmse | rsq | lowest | below_zero | |:------------------|-------:|------:|---------:|-------------:| | Straight line | 4.9 | 0.23 | -1.88 | 1 | | Curve | 4.73 | 0.29 | -1.45 | 10 | | Poisson | 4.82 | 0.25 | 0.3 | 0 | | Negative binomial | 4.8 | 0.26 | 0.28 | 0 | ::: ::: ::: The two count models make no negative predictions; the lowest is 0.23 animals. They also score a little better than the linear regression curve on new sites: $R^2$ rises from 0.22 to 0.24 for Poisson and 0.25 for the negative binomial. Poisson and the negative binomial predict almost the same counts; what the negative binomial changes is how sure the model is. ## The same design for other outcomes All three models on this page and the last share one design: a weighted sum of the inputs, turned into a prediction by a function that keeps it in range. For linear regression the function does nothing; for counts it is $e$ raised to the sum, which keeps the prediction above zero. [Logistic regression](logistic-regression.qmd) uses the same design for a probability, which must stay between 0 and 1. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Poisson regression predicts the log of the expected count, so its predictions never fall below zero. - Its coefficients read as multipliers once raised as a power of $e$: on the survey, a muddy station holds 1.34 times the count of a sandy one. - Poisson assumes the counts vary as much as their average and no more; here they vary about 3.7 times as much, so its confidence intervals are too narrow. - The negative binomial allows for the extra spread. Its predictions match Poisson's, and its wider intervals no longer tell rock from sand. - Match the model to the outcome: a count is never negative, and its spread grows with its size. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Fit `poisson_reg()` with `line_recipe` instead of `curve_recipe` and add it to the figure. It is a straight line in the log of the count: what shape is it on the figure? 2. Compute the spread ratio for the negative binomial, with `nb_fit` in place of `poisson_glm`. Is it closer to 1?
